templates.scenario: You work as {role|a} at {workplace|a} and are completing {document|a}. It says: "Finish by 4 p.m. Friday. Contact the customer by email. Do not replace any parts without supervisor approval." While working, you find a part that is cracked.
templates.prompt: What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Ask your {lead} to approve replacing the part, and note the crack on {document|the}.
options.why: The document requires supervisor approval before any part is replaced, so getting it first and noting the problem follows it exactly.

options.text: Replace the part right away so the job is finished by 4 p.m. as the document asks.
options.why: The deadline matters, but the document also says not to replace parts without supervisor approval. Both instructions have to be followed.
options.misconception: Meeting the deadline matters more than the other instructions.

options.text: Finish the job with the cracked part and leave it off {document|the}, so nothing delays the deadline.
options.why: Leaving a known problem unreported hides something the supervisor and customer would want to know about.
options.misconception: If the part still works, it is not worth mentioning.

options.text: Call the customer to ask whether you can replace the part, since it is their property.
options.why: The document names the supervisor as the person who approves, and says the customer should be contacted by email.
options.misconception: Anyone connected to the job can give approval.

templates.principle: Read the whole document and follow every instruction in it, including who must approve what.

templates.scenario: You spot several mismatched figures in {document|a} that {coworker} wrote. It goes out later today. You decide to send a short message to {coworker}.
templates.prompt: Which message is the most appropriate?

options.text: Hi {coworker}, I noticed three places where the numbers do not match. Could we check them together before it goes out?
options.why: This message is specific about the problem, polite in tone, and suggests working together before the deadline.

options.text: This document is full of mistakes and has to be completely redone before anyone sees it, so please fix it right now.
options.why: This is harsh and exaggerated, and it does not say where the problems are, which makes them harder to fix.
options.misconception: Blunt criticism is the clearest way to communicate.

options.text: Hey, there might be some issues here or there, so maybe look it over at some point if you get a chance.
options.why: This is so vague that it does not say what the problem is or that the document goes out today.
options.misconception: A gentle hint is more polite than a specific message.

options.text: Yo, this is kinda messed up lol, numbers are off in a few spots, fix it when you can.
options.why: Slang and joking can sound careless in a work message, and it does not mention the deadline.
options.misconception: Casual wording keeps the conversation friendly.

templates.principle: Write to your audience: be specific about the problem, keep a respectful tone, and mention what matters, such as deadlines.

review.notes: Message options are all realistic workplace phrasings.

templates.scenario: {coworker} sends this message to the team.
templates.prompt: Tap the line that is not clear enough.

segments.text: The delivery arrives tomorrow at 9:00 a.m.
segments.whyFine: This line gives a specific day and time.

segments.text: Please put the boxes away in the right spot soon.
segments.why: "Right spot" and "soon" do not say where or by when, so readers have to guess.

templates.principle: Clear instructions name the place, the action and the time instead of words like 'soon' or 'right spot'.

templates.scenario: You need to send your {lead} an email about a schedule change at {workplace|the}.
templates.prompt: Put these writing steps in a sensible order.

steps.text: Decide the main point you need to communicate
Write the email with a clear subject line and short sentences

precedence.why: Knowing the main point keeps the message focused.
You can only proofread a message that has been written.
Sending before proofreading means mistakes reach the reader.

templates.principle: Write with purpose: decide your point, write clearly, proofread, then send.

templates.scenario: {Client|a} sends an upset email to {workplace|the} that mixes a complaint, a question about a deadline, and a request for a refund. You have been asked to reply, and you have only skimmed the first paragraph.

options.text: Read the whole email again and list exactly what the person is asking before you start your reply.
options.why: A message that mixes several points can only be answered fully if you know every question in it. Listing them first keeps your reply complete and clear.

options.text: Start writing a reply as soon as you finish the first paragraph so that it goes out quickly.
options.why: Replying to part of a message can miss the deadline question or the refund request, which creates follow-up emails and more frustration.
options.misconception: A fast reply is better than a complete one.

options.text: Forward the email to your {lead} without reading it carefully, so someone else can deal with it.
options.why: You were asked to reply. Passing it along unread adds delay and gives your {lead} no summary.
options.misconception: Passing it on is the safest response.

options.text: Reply to the loudest complaint and assume the other questions will be answered along the way.
options.why: Questions about deadlines and refunds will not be answered unless you address them. Readers expect each point to be covered.
options.misconception: Answering the most emotional part covers everything.

templates.principle: Read a document fully and list what it asks for before you write your response.
templates.timing: Reading and listing the asks comes before drafting.

templates.scenario: A work order says to email a customer a delivery estimate by noon. A newer note says not to share any date until inventory is confirmed; the system will update in an hour. Your lead is responsible for clarifying order instructions, and the customer has asked for an update.
templates.prompt: What is the clearest and most responsible response?

options.text: Tell your lead the directions conflict, ask which controls, then update the customer using verified details.
options.why: This reports the conflict to the person authorized to resolve it and avoids sharing an unconfirmed date.

options.text: Tell the customer you are checking the order and will follow up when you have a confirmed update.
options.why: This acknowledges the customer without guessing, but the conflict still needs to be raised with the lead.
options.misconception: A useful preliminary step is mistaken for a complete plan.

options.text: Send the estimate by noon because the work order is the main document and gives a specific deadline.
options.why: The newer note explicitly withholds a date until inventory is confirmed; choosing one direction without clarification risks misleading the customer.
options.misconception: The most prominent instruction automatically overrides a conflicting note.

options.text: Wait silently for the system update, then send a date without telling anyone that the directions conflicted.
options.why: This leaves the noon communication expectation unaddressed and does not resolve the conflict for future work.

templates.principle: When instructions conflict, name the specific conflict, ask an authorized person to clarify, and communicate only verified information.

review.notes: The two instructions conflict, inventory is unconfirmed, and the lead is explicitly authorized to clarify before the customer receives an estimate.

templates.scenario: You are asked to write an update stating when and how many replacement parts were delivered. The shared log lists a quantity of 18 but has no date. The original receiving record may contain the date, and your supervisor can access it.

options.text: Check the original receiving record or ask your supervisor to confirm the date before writing the complete update.
options.why: The shared log supports the quantity but not the date, so the missing fact must be verified before it is reported.

options.text: Draft the update with the verified quantity and mark the delivery date as awaiting confirmation.
options.why: This separates known from unknown information, but checking the available source first may let you provide the complete update.
options.misconception: A useful preliminary step is mistaken for a complete plan.

options.text: Use the date from a similar delivery last week because the quantity and supplier are the same.
options.why: A similar transaction does not establish the date of this delivery.
options.misconception: A nearby example can replace the source record.

options.text: Guess a date based on when the parts were expected and send the update before the deadline.
options.why: An expected date is not proof the delivery occurred then; this presents a guess as a fact.
options.misconception: Meeting a deadline justifies filling a missing fact.

templates.principle: Separate verified facts from missing information and check the source before writing a factual update.

review.notes: The log includes quantity but omits the date; the original receiving record is identified as a possible source and the supervisor can verify it.

templates.timing: Verify the absent date before drafting it as a confirmed fact.

templates.scenario: A purchaser expects an accurate answer about a shipment before close of business. Your group sends external notices, and the signed receipt is stored with the receiving team. Arrange the actions so the final response is dependable.
templates.prompt: Arrange the steps so the message is accurate and complete before it is sent.

steps.text: Read both records and identify exactly which quantity conflicts
Check the original receiving record or ask the responsible lead to confirm the quantity
Draft the update using only the confirmed quantity and other verified details
Proofread for accuracy, clarity, and the customer's actual question
Send the checked update through the approved customer channel

precedence.why: The conflicting value must be identified before it can be checked.
The message should use the confirmed value, not an unresolved figure.
The draft must exist before its accuracy and clarity can be checked.
Proofreading and channel checks happen before sending.

templates.principle: Resolve factual conflicts at their source, then draft, review, and send a clear response through the proper channel.

review.notes: The evidence conflict, verification source, audience, and sending channel are stated.

templates.scenario: A team lead reviews four handoff notes before assigning work for the next shift.
templates.prompt: Select the note that is too ambiguous for a reliable handoff.

segments.text: The replacement filter is in cabinet 2; Maya will install it before the 3 p.m. equipment check.
segments.whyFine: It names the item, location, responsible person, and deadline.

segments.text: Two customer forms need a second review; send them to the quality desk before noon.
segments.whyFine: It states the task, destination, and time.

segments.text: The damaged cart is tagged by the loading door; do not use it until the lead checks it.
segments.whyFine: It identifies the hazard, location, and restriction.

segments.text: Take care of the other issue soon, and let everyone know when it is handled.
segments.why: The note does not identify which issue, who should handle it, or what deadline applies, so the next shift cannot act reliably.

templates.principle: A useful handoff states the task, responsible person or channel, location, and timing needed for the next action.

review.notes: Only one note lacks enough information to identify and complete its assigned action.
